First-year breeders of the Great northern loon (Gavia immer) typically lay two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch], and a pair will successfully fledge young from only a single brood per year [F_R_i = single brood per year], resulting in a maximum reproduction rate of 2 eggs per year [Ri = 2 eggs per year] at the body temperature of 39.3 °C [T = 39.3 °C] that characterizes this active, pursuit-diving species. The chicks emerge from eggs after an incubation period of approximately 24.5 days [ab = approximately 24.5 days], which is documented under artificial incubation conditions maintained precisely at 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. Upon hatching, these semi-precocial young are wet from the egg but quickly dry into a dense downy coat. Unlike many altricial birds that hatch naked and helpless, loon chicks enter the world with their eyes open and are capable of swimming within hours of exiting the shell. Their initial body wet weight at birth averages 79.6 grams [Wwb = 79.6 grams], a measure that reflects the substantial yolk reserves that sustained them through the final stages of development within the calcareous egg. This modest starting mass contrasts sharply with the impressive adult proportions they will eventually attain, setting the stage for a rapid growth trajectory sustained by intensive parental provisioning of small fish.

As the nestling chick develops through its early weeks, it undergoes a period of rapid mass gain that is heavily dependent upon the diligent food delivery efforts of both parents. The downy young spend much of their early life riding on the backs of the adults, a behavior that provides both warmth and protection from aquatic predators. The time since birth at fledging, marking the point at which the young bird achieves its first flight and gains full feather maturation, has been recorded at approximately 73.5 days [tx = approximately 73.5 days], a developmental milestone that is associated with the species' typical active body temperature of 39.3 °C [T = 39.3 °C]. This relatively lengthy nestling and prefledging period is characteristic of large-bodied divers, reflecting the considerable time required to develop the powerful flight muscles and fully grown wing feathers necessary for sustained flight. Upon achieving independence, the fledgling will gradually become less dependent on its parents for food and protection, eventually dispersing from the natal territory to find its own lake or coastal foraging grounds during the late summer and autumn months before winter migration.

The juvenile bird, now independent, enters a sub-adult phase that spans the next several seasons, during which it must learn to efficiently capture prey and establish a territory of its own. Puberty, marking the onset of gonadal maturation and the initiation of gametogenesis, is estimated to occur at roughly 220.5 days since birth [tp = roughly 220.5 days since birth] when measured at the typical body temperature of 39.3 °C [T = 39.3 °C]. However, this physiological readiness does not immediately translate into successful reproduction. Loons are known to delay their first breeding attempt considerably, as competition for high-quality nesting territories on large, fish-rich lakes is intense. The time since birth at first brood, representing the age at which an individual successfully hatches its first clutch, is documented at 730.0 days since birth [tR = 730.0 days since birth] under the same thermal conditions at a temperature of 39.3 °C [T = 39.3 °C]. This multi-year delay before first reproduction is a common life-history strategy among long-lived seabirds and divers, allowing the immature bird to accumulate sufficient body reserves and foraging experience to sustain the high energetic costs of egg production and chick rearing.

Upon reaching full adulthood, the breeding bird attains its ultimate body proportions, with the maximum recorded total length from the tip of the bill to the end of the tail measuring 80.0 centimeters [Li = 80.0 centimeters]. This substantial body size is accompanied by a correspondingly impressive ultimate wet weight for a fully grown adult of 4040.0 grams [Wwi = 4040.0 grams], a mass that places Gavia immer among the largest of the world's loon species. This heavy body is an adaptation for efficient deep diving, as the added weight reduces buoyancy and allows the bird to pursue prey such as perch and sculpin at depths exceeding fifty meters. The body mass of an adult loon fluctuates throughout the year, however, being at its lowest during the incubation period when adults fast for extended stretches and at its highest just prior to fall migration, when hyperphagia leads to the accumulation of thick fat reserves that fuel the long journey to wintering grounds along both the Atlantic and Pacific coasts.

Despite these impressive physical attributes, the species is characterized by a remarkably slow life history that is typical of large-bodied, long-lived waterbirds. The maximum recorded lifespan for a wild Great northern loon has been placed at approximately 8797.0 days [am = approximately 8797.0 days], a figure that corresponds to roughly 24 years of life when maintained at the typical body temperature of 39.3 °C [T = 39.3 °C]. Banding returns from long-term monitoring programs on lakes in Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Ontario have confirmed that individuals can persist for over two decades, often returning to the same territory and the same mate year after year. This extended longevity is offset by low annual productivity, with most pairs successfully fledging only a single chick per year at best, and complete reproductive failure being common during years of severe weather, fluctuating water levels, or diminished prey availability. Consequently, population persistence depends heavily on the high annual survival rates of the breeding adults, a classic bet-hedging strategy among long-lived vertebrates that buffers against periodic recruitment failures.

The migration behavior of Gavia immer further underscores its life-history strategy, as individuals undertake annual movements from breeding lakes in the northern United States and Canada to coastal wintering areas along the Atlantic and Pacific seaboards, covering distances of several thousand kilometers. During these migrations, loons rely on fat reserves accumulated prior to departure, and stopover sites along major river systems and Great Lakes shorelines provide critical refueling opportunities. Comparative studies within the family Gaviidae suggest that the energetic demands of migration, combined with the sustained pursuit diving required for foraging, impose a high metabolic cost that is reflected in the species' relatively low reproductive output per year. The trade-off between longevity and annual fecundity observed in Gavia immer mirrors patterns seen in other long-lived, slow-reproducing seabirds such as albatrosses and procellariids, emphasizing the role of environmental predictability in shaping avian life histories.
